claim: For an apex domain on external DNS with no ALIAS/ANAME support, Netlify documents a single A record to 75.2.60.5
detail:
At your DNS provider, edit two records and leave everything else untouched.

1) Apex. Replace the existing Wix A record (host `@` or blank, value 185.230.63.107) with a single A record: host `@` (or blank if the provider does not accept `@`), type A, value 75.2.60.5, TTL 600. Edit the existing record in place, or delete it and add the new one in the same sitting — never leave both values live, or DNS round-robins between Wix and Netlify and roughly half of visitors get the old site.

If your provider does support ALIAS, ANAME, or flattened CNAME, prefer that instead of the A record: host `@`, target `apex-loadbalancer.netlify.com`. Netlify calls this "more resilient than the fallback option", and the A record is the documented fallback for providers that have no ALIAS type.

2) www. Replace the existing Wix CNAME (host `www`, value `pointing.wixdns.net`) with a CNAME: host `www`, value your site's Netlify subdomain, `<your-site-name>.netlify.app` — not apex-loadbalancer, and not 75.2.60.5. Netlify automatically adds the www subdomain when you assign an apex domain, and it needs its own CNAME. Skipping this leaves www on Wix.

3) Before you save either record, open your Netlify dashboard's "Pending DNS verification" modal for this domain. If it shows a customized IP or a customized load-balancer hostname — it does for sites on High-Performance Edge — use that value rather than 75.2.60.5 or apex-loadbalancer.netlify.com.

4) Do not touch anything else in the zone. Leave every MX record, every SPF/DKIM/DMARC TXT record, and any autodiscover or autoconfig entry exactly as they are; this migration does not affect mail, and deleting or re-creating those records is what takes business email down. If the panel offers a "reset to defaults" or "remove all records" action, do not use it.

5) Keep TTL low (600) through cutover, verify with `dig +short yourdomain.com A` (expect 75.2.60.5) and `dig +short www.yourdomain.com CNAME`, wait for Netlify to issue the certificate, then raise TTL back to 3600 once the site is confirmed good.

Source: https://docs.netlify.com/manage/domains/configure-domains/configure-external-dns/ (TTL values above are operational guidance; Netlify's page does not specify a TTL).

claim: Verification command to confirm the IP is still current before you paste it
detail:
Before you paste anything, confirm the IP — but treat the docs and your Netlify dashboard as the authority, not dig.

1. Read the value from Netlify's own page: https://docs.netlify.com/manage/domains/configure-domains/configure-external-dns/ (not the troubleshooting-tips page, which does not list an IP). It currently reads: "Point the record to Netlify's load balancer IP address: 75.2.60.5".

2. Read the value Netlify shows for YOUR site: in Netlify, Domain management > Production domains > "Pending DNS verification" next to pianotuningscy.com. This is the authoritative value for your project — some plans (High-Performance Edge) are given a different dedicated target.

3. Optional sanity check: `dig +short apex-loadbalancer.netlify.com A`. Note this returns MORE THAN ONE address (today: 99.83.231.61 and 75.2.60.5, in varying order). Do NOT paste "whatever it returns" — you are only confirming that 75.2.60.5 still appears in the list. If 75.2.60.5 is absent, or the dashboard shows something different, stop and use the dashboard value; do not invent an A record from dig output. (apex-loadbalancer.netlify.com is documented as an ALIAS/ANAME/flattened-CNAME target, not as a source for A values. one.com's DNS panel has no ALIAS/ANAME, so you use the A record 75.2.60.5.)

After cutover, verify (add @1.1.1.1 to bypass a cached local resolver):
- `dig +short pianotuningscy.com A` → expect 75.2.60.5 only (today it still shows 185.230.63.107, the Wix address)
- `dig +short www.pianotuningscy.com CNAME` → expect your-project.netlify.app. (with trailing dot; today it still shows www43.wixdns.net.)
- `dig +short MX pianotuningscy.com` → MUST still return all four: mx1, mx2, mx3, mx4.mailpod15-cph3.g1i.one.com (priority 10 each). If any are missing, email is broken — restore them before anything else.
- `curl -sSI https://pianotuningscy.com | head -20` and `curl -sSI https://www.pianotuningscy.com | head -20`
Allow up to 24-48 hours for full propagation; check the MX line first and at every step.

claim: The www CNAME target is your project's own netlify.app subdomain, not a shared Netlify hostname
detail: Create: host `www`, type CNAME, value `<your-project-name>.netlify.app` — the exact name is shown in your Netlify dashboard (Project configuration → Domain management) and is per-project, so read it there rather than guessing; it may be an auto-generated name like `brave-curie-12345.netlify.app` or one you renamed. Type it without a trailing dot unless your DNS panel explicitly shows existing records with one — most panels append it automatically and some reject a value that includes it. This replaces the current CNAME to www43.wixdns.net. There is no generic "www.netlify.com" target. If the project is on High-Performance Edge, Netlify's docs say to point the record to the dedicated subdomain in your High-Performance Edge onboarding PDF instead. Two things to do alongside it: (a) Netlify automatically adds the apex domain to the project once www is configured, so the bare domain needs its own record too — an ALIAS/ANAME/flattened CNAME to the same `<your-project-name>.netlify.app` if your provider supports it, otherwise the A record to Netlify's load balancer IP shown in your dashboard; without it the bare domain will not resolve. (b) Change only the www record. Leave every MX record and every mail-related TXT/CNAME (SPF, DKIM, DMARC, autodiscover/autoconfig) exactly as they are — business email does not go through this record and editing those is what takes mail down.

claim: Netlify strongly recommends making www the primary domain when DNS stays external — this is the single biggest performance decision here
detail:
Netlify's docs do strongly recommend making www your primary domain when DNS stays with an external provider. Per https://docs.netlify.com/manage/domains/get-started-with-domains/: with external DNS providers Netlify "strongly recommend[s] making a www subdomain ... your primary domain instead of the apex domain," because an apex on third-party DNS can't take advantage of direct DNS routing on Netlify's global CDN. With Netlify DNS instead, apex and www "perform equally well."

Setup, corrected: set www.pianotuningscy.com as the primary domain in Netlify, and add a CNAME for www pointing to your site's Netlify subdomain (the <your-site>.netlify.app hostname shown in your Netlify site settings — use the real value, not a placeholder).

For the apex, check what your DNS provider supports before typing anything:
- If it supports ALIAS, ANAME, or flattened CNAME records, use that record type pointed at apex-loadbalancer.netlify.com. This is Netlify's recommended configuration and the docs call it "more resilient than the fallback option."
- Only if your provider supports none of those, use the fallback: an A record for the apex pointing to 75.2.60.5. That IP is current and correct, but it is the fallback, not the recommendation — the original instruction skipped straight to it.

Netlify then redirects the apex to www automatically ("If you set the www subdomain as your primary domain, Netlify will automatically redirect the apex domain to the www subdomain"). The docs do not state the redirect's status code, so don't promise a 301 specifically.

Leave every MX record and every mail-related TXT record (SPF, DKIM, DMARC) exactly as they are — none of the above touches business email. Change only the apex A/ALIAS record and the www record.

claim: Netlify does recommend moving nameservers to Netlify DNS, but for this domain the MX records make external DNS the safer choice
detail: Netlify labels Netlify DNS "Most recommended" (Get started with domains, updated Mar 18, 2026) and lists the gains: a wildcard SSL certificate covering every branch subdomain, apex served over the CDN, custom subdomains for Deploy Previews and branch deploys, and standalone subdomain delegation. Against that, the Set up Netlify DNS page (updated Mar 21, 2026) warns: "If you have any existing records on your current DNS provider, such as MX records for email service, make sure to copy them to Netlify DNS first." And the Why Netlify DNS page (updated Jan 24, 2026) states: "Netlify does not allow inbound DNS zone transfers. If you have a lot of existing DNS records, it's simplest and safest to use an external DNS provider." This domain has four MX records (mx1–mx4.mailpod15-cph3.g1i.one.com, priority 10) plus an ftp CNAME, all of which would have to be retyped by hand. Recommendation: leave the nameservers at one.com (ns01/ns02.one.com) and change only the apex and www records. Per Netlify's external-DNS page (updated Oct 28, 2025), the apex should ideally be an ALIAS, ANAME, or flattened CNAME to apex-loadbalancer.netlify.com; one.com's panel does not offer those types, so use the documented fallback — an A record on @ pointing to 75.2.60.5 — and set www as a CNAME to your <sitename>.netlify.app target. Read both values off the "Pending DNS verification" modal in your Netlify dashboard immediately before typing them, since High-Performance Edge sites use different load-balancer values. Confirm the four MX records and the ftp CNAME are present in the one.com zone before and after the edit; you never touch the MX rows, so business email is structurally untouched. Move to Netlify DNS later only as a deliberate, separately planned migration if you want wildcard certs for branch deploys.

claim: Let's Encrypt certificates are provisioned automatically, but only AFTER DNS points at Netlify and the old TTL has expired — the order is strict
detail:
Let's Encrypt certificates are provisioned automatically, but only after DNS points at Netlify and the old cached records have expired. The order is strict:

(1) Add pianotuningscy.com and www.pianotuningscy.com to the Netlify project FIRST. Because you are keeping the zone at one.com (external DNS), the applicable doc is Configure external DNS, not Netlify DNS: "you must first add the domain to your site on Netlify and then create a CNAME record with your DNS provider." Do NOT follow the Netlify DNS instructions and do NOT change your nameservers at one.com — delegating the zone to Netlify would drop your existing MX records and take business email down.

(2) Then change the records at one.com: at the apex, use an ALIAS/ANAME/flattened CNAME to apex-loadbalancer.netlify.com if one.com supports it, otherwise an A record to 75.2.60.5; for www, a CNAME to [your-site-name].netlify.app. Leave MX, TXT/SPF, DKIM and any mail-related records untouched.

(3) Then wait. Netlify must validate that the DNS records point at it before it can issue: "All previous DNS settings must have their cache timeouts expired. The TTL setting on a DNS record determines how long the record may be cached, and this cache must expire before your new DNS settings can be validated for certificate provisioning." The relevant TTL is whatever was in effect BEFORE you edited the record, so if your apex was already at 600s caches clear in roughly 10 minutes, but Netlify still needs the records propagated globally and the docs allow up to 24-48 hours. If the first issuance attempt fails, Netlify retries every 10 minutes for the first 24 hours, then once an hour for the following two days; if no cert exists after 24 hours, assume a DNS misconfiguration rather than waiting longer.

Renewal is fully automatic for Netlify-managed certificates. Check status in Domain management > HTTPS. Do not enable Force HTTPS until the certificate shows as issued.

Optional hardening: add a CAA record, but use the value Netlify documents, which pins its Let's Encrypt account rather than the whole CA:
0 issue "letsencrypt.org;accounturi=https://acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/acme/acct/54403714"
A bare 0 issue "letsencrypt.org" also works but is weaker. Add the CAA record only after the certificate has issued, since a malformed CAA record will block issuance.

claim: Exact records to change at one.com — two edits, nothing else
detail:
Two edits at one.com, nothing else.

EDIT 1 — apex (@ / blank host): first look at what record types one.com's DNS editor offers. If it has ALIAS, ANAME or "CNAME flattening", use that and point it at apex-loadbalancer.netlify.com. If it only has A, change the existing apex A record from 185.230.63.107 (Wix) to 75.2.60.5. Either way, exactly one apex record — do not add a second A record, and never an apex CNAME (a CNAME cannot coexist with the MX records at the apex; that would break your email). TTL 600 if the field is editable (one.com defaults to 3600); Netlify itself does not specify a TTL.

EDIT 2 — www: change the CNAME value from www43.wixdns.net to your site's own Netlify subdomain, e.g. your-site-name.netlify.app — the exact name shown in your Netlify dashboard, not a guess.

LEAVE UNTOUCHED: the four MX records, the ftp CNAME, and the NS records (ns01/ns02.one.com). Touching MX or NS is what takes email down.

Before typing anything, open Netlify → Domain management → Production domains → "Pending DNS verification" next to your domain and use the values shown there. Those are site-specific and override the generic doc values — in particular, sites on Netlify's High-Performance Edge get a different apex load balancer and a different subdomain target.

One caveat on the plan itself: Netlify notes that an apex domain served this way always resolves to a single load balancer IP and so cannot use direct CDN routing, and recommends making www.yourdomain the primary domain with the apex redirecting to it. That is a configuration choice in Netlify, not a DNS edit, and does not change either record above.

claim: Free tier: a new account today gets the CREDIT-based Free plan — 300 credits/month, hard limit — not the old 100 GB / 300 build-minutes plan
detail: Accounts created on or after 4 September 2025 are on credit-based pricing; only pre-existing accounts keep the legacy plan (100 GB bandwidth, 300 build minutes). You would be signing up today, so you get: 300 credits/month, hard limit, no auto-recharge; 1 concurrent build; 500 projects; 1 team owner; no password protection; no private-repo support (your repo is public, so fine). Current rates after the April 2026 update: bandwidth 20 credits/GB, production deploy 15 credits flat (build minutes are no longer metered at all), web requests 2 credits per 10,000, form submissions now free, deploy previews and branch deploys free. So 300 credits is roughly 15 GB of bandwidth OR 20 production deploys per month in isolation, and in practice a mix of both. Custom domains with SSL and unlimited deploy previews are included on Free. Verify the live numbers at the pricing page before committing, since these rates changed as recently as April 2026.

claim: On the credit Free plan, exhausting credits PAUSES the site — visitors see a 'Site not available' page
detail: Netlify's billing FAQ: "Once your monthly credit allotment is used up for all web projects on your team, all of your web projects (sites/apps) are paused and visitors to your web projects will find a `Site not available` page at each of your web project's URLs." No new web requests, no form submissions processed, no new production deploys — until the next billing cycle or an upgrade. For a real business whose customers book tunings through the site, this is an outage risk, not an abstract quota. Mitigation: put a card on file / move to the Personal plan ($9/mo) before cutover, or at minimum set up the usage alerts and watch the first full month. Netlify notifies at 50%, 75%, 90% and 100%.

claim: (d) What GitHub Pages DOES support for a custom apex domain: four A records, four AAAA records, or an ALIAS/ANAME to <user>.github.io.
detail: For a custom apex domain, GitHub Pages supports either four A records — 185.199.108.153, 185.199.109.153, 185.199.110.153, 185.199.111.153 — or four AAAA records — 2606:50c0:8000::153, 2606:50c0:8001::153, 2606:50c0:8002::153, 2606:50c0:8003::153 — or both, or an ALIAS/ANAME record pointing the apex at <user>.github.io if the DNS provider offers one. one.com's DNS editor does not generally offer ALIAS/ANAME, so plan on the four A records (adding the four AAAA records as well is optional and safe). Confirm the current values on the GitHub docs page immediately before editing DNS; `dig +short <user>.github.io A` is a useful cross-check of the Pages edge IPs, but note it returns the same addresses for any *.github.io name and therefore does not prove a particular site exists. Add or edit only A/AAAA records at the apex and leave every MX and TXT (SPF/DKIM/DMARC) record untouched — those carry the business email and are not affected by the site migration.

claim: (d) www target, CNAME file, and the automatic www→apex redirect.
detail:
(d) www target, CNAME file, and the www->apex redirect — verified, with two clarifications.

www CNAME: `www.pianotuningscy.com` CNAME -> `andy-arrow.github.io` (replacing `www43.wixdns.net`). Per GitHub: "The CNAME record should always point to `<user>.github.io` or `<organization>.github.io`, excluding the repository name." Enter exactly `andy-arrow.github.io` — no `/pianotuningscy` path, no `https://`. (Do not touch MX, or any TXT/CNAME records used for mail — SPF, DKIM, DMARC, autodiscover. Only the A records for the apex and the www CNAME change.)

CNAME file: "The CNAME filename must be all uppercase" and "The CNAME file can contain only one domain." This does not apply here: this repo publishes from a custom GitHub Actions workflow (.github/workflows/deploy.yml), and GitHub states "no CNAME file is created, and any existing CNAME file is ignored and is not required." The domain is read from Settings > Pages > Custom domain instead, so it must be typed there for the site to answer on the custom domain at all.

www -> apex redirect — CLARIFICATION: the redirect follows whichever domain is entered in Settings > Pages, not a fixed www->apex rule. GitHub: "If you configure www.example.com as the custom domain ... then example.com will redirect to www.example.com. If you instead configure example.com as the custom domain, then www.example.com will redirect to example.com." To get the stated www->apex behaviour, enter `pianotuningscy.com` (apex, no www) as the custom domain, and have both the apex A records and the www CNAME in DNS. Entering `www.pianotuningscy.com` there would redirect the other way.

SEPARATE BLOCKER, not a DNS value — check before switching DNS: deploy.yml currently builds this site in review mode, with PREVIEW_BASE=/pianotuningscy, PREVIEW_SITE=https://andy-arrow.github.io and PUBLIC_PREVIEW=true, which the workflow's own comment says is "marked noindex sitewide and banner-flagged." If DNS is pointed at Pages while the workflow still builds that way, pianotuningscy.com will serve a noindexed, banner-flagged site with asset and link paths under /pianotuningscy/ — broken styling and links, and invisible to Google. Change the workflow to a production build at the apex domain and confirm the deployed result before repointing DNS.

claim: (d) Enforce HTTPS is supported and free, but is fragile about stray DNS records and needs a Let's Encrypt CAA record if any CAA records exist.
detail:
(d) Enforce HTTPS is supported and free, but it is fragile about stray DNS records, and if you have any CAA records one of them must allow Let's Encrypt.

"All GitHub Pages sites, including sites that are correctly configured with a custom domain, support HTTPS and HTTPS enforcement." Enable it at repo Settings > Pages > Enforce HTTPS, after the automatic DNS check that begins when you set the custom domain has passed.

Timing: certificate issuance usually takes minutes. GitHub says "It can take up to an hour for your site to become available over HTTPS after you configure your custom domain." Do not wait a day — if the process has not completed several minutes after you clicked Save, click Remove next to the custom domain, retype it, and click Save again; this cancels and restarts provisioning.

The caveat that bites on one.com: an HTTPS certificate can fail to generate because of "extra DNS records, or records not pointing to the IP addresses for GitHub Pages." This applies to records on the apex (@) and www. The existing ftp.pianotuningscy.com CNAME to one.com is an unrelated subdomain and is fine; leftover Wix A or CNAME records on the apex or www are not, and must be deleted.

CAA: the requirement is conditional — "If you're using Certification Authority Authorization (CAA) records, at least one CAA record must exist with the value letsencrypt.org for your site to be accessible over HTTPS." pianotuningscy.com currently has no CAA records at all, which is fine (no CAA means any CA may issue). Do not add one. If you ever add a CAA record, it must include letsencrypt.org or HTTPS will break.

Wildcards: GitHub "strongly recommend[s] that you do not use wildcard DNS records, such as *.example.com."

Sources: the HTTPS support statement, the Enforce HTTPS path, the extra-DNS-records caveat and the Remove/retype remedy are at https://docs.github.com/en/pages/getting-started-with-github-pages/securing-your-github-pages-site-with-https ; the one-hour timing, the CAA requirement and the wildcard recommendation are at https://docs.github.com/en/pages/configuring-a-custom-domain-for-your-github-pages-site/troubleshooting-custom-domains-and-github-pages

claim: VERDICT: GitHub Pages is not viable as the production host for this site as built. Netlify (or Cloudflare Pages) is.
detail:
VERDICT (unchanged): GitHub Pages cannot host this site as built; Netlify is the right production host. Corrections:

1. HSTS — the claim understates the loss. A GitHub Pages site on a CUSTOM domain sends no Strict-Transport-Security header at all; GitHub's docs say HSTS is enforced for *.github.io subdomains only, and a live check of a Pages custom-domain site (jekyllrb.com) returns only `server: GitHub.com` and `cache-control: max-age=600`. So ALL seven headers in netlify.toml are lost, not "all except GitHub's own weaker HSTS". That fixed `max-age=600` also confirms the second half: there is no way to set `Cache-Control: immutable` on /_astro/*.

2. Cited source — https://docs.github.com/en/pages/getting-started-with-github-pages/github-pages-limits does not support any of this. It covers only 1 GB repo/site size, 10-min build timeout, 10 builds/hour, 100 GB/month bandwidth, plus a prohibited-uses note (no commercial SaaS, no sensitive transactions). Cite instead .../what-is-github-pages (static-only definition) and the observed 405-on-POST.

3. Cloudflare Pages is NOT "the same shape" of DNS change — this is the one line that could cost the business its email. Cloudflare's docs state that for an apex/root domain the nameservers must be moved to Cloudflare ("configure your nameservers to point to Cloudflare's nameservers"), after which Cloudflare creates the CNAME itself; only subdomains work from external DNS, and adding a CNAME without first registering the domain in the Pages dashboard produces a 522. Moving nameservers off one.com means re-creating the four MX records and the ftp record in Cloudflare's zone by hand — a live-mailbox risk the Netlify path does not carry. Cloudflare Pages is a drop-in for the _redirects/_headers files, not for the DNS step.

4. Exact one.com values for the Netlify path. one.com supports A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT, SRV, TLSA, SSHFP, CAA, DS, NS — no ALIAS/ANAME — so Netlify's preferred apex target `apex-loadbalancer.netlify.com` is unavailable and the documented fallback applies:
   - Apex: change the A record for @ from 185.230.63.107 to 75.2.60.5 (Netlify's load-balancer IP, docs.netlify.com/manage/domains/configure-domains/configure-external-dns/).
   - www: change the CNAME for www from www43.wixdns.net to <your-site-name>.netlify.app.
   - Leave untouched: the four MX records (mx1–mx4.mailpod15-cph3.g1i.one.com), the ftp record, and the one.com nameservers.
   Add the domain in the Netlify dashboard before or at the same time as the DNS edit so the Let's Encrypt certificate provisions; allow up to 48h for propagation.

5. One extra step the repo's README understates: Netlify Forms does not work "untouched" on a new site — form detection must be switched on once in the Netlify UI (Forms > Enable form detection) and the site redeployed, otherwise the enquiry form posts into nothing.

claim: If GitHub Pages is used anyway (e.g. as a temporary stopgap), four repo changes are required before the domain is pointed at it.
detail:
If GitHub Pages is used as a stopgap, four things must change before the domain is pointed at it.

1) Stop the preview build. In .github/workflows/deploy.yml, delete the three env lines under "Build (preview mode)": PREVIEW_SITE, PREVIEW_BASE and PUBLIC_PREVIEW. Do not edit astro.config.mjs — it has no hardcoded base; it derives base and site from those variables. Removing them simultaneously drops the /pianotuningscy base path, removes the noindex meta and the review banner, re-enables the sitemap integration and the production robots.txt, and re-enables Plausible. Leave `SITE` in astro.config.mjs and `url` in src/data/site.ts as https://www.pianotuningscy.com.

2) Match the custom domain to that hostname. In Settings > Pages set the custom domain to www.pianotuningscy.com and create one DNS record: CNAME www -> andy-arrow.github.io. This is the simpler and safer cutover because it touches no apex record and therefore cannot disturb the MX records carrying the business email. If the apex is wanted instead, it needs all four A records (185.199.108.153, 185.199.109.153, 185.199.110.153, 185.199.111.153) and all four AAAA records (2606:50c0:8000::153, 2606:50c0:8001::153, 2606:50c0:8002::153, 2606:50c0:8003::153) added as new records alongside the existing MX and TXT/SPF entries — never replacing them — plus a www CNAME, since GitHub auto-redirects www to the apex but the site's own canonical URLs are www. Because the deploy runs from a custom Actions workflow, no CNAME file is created and any existing one is ignored; the domain is read from Settings. Then wait for the DNS check to pass and tick Enforce HTTPS — the option can take up to 24 hours to appear, and HTTPS up to an hour to work after that; if it stalls, remove and re-add the custom domain.

3) Repoint the contact form. Set `endpoint` in src/data/site.ts to a real third-party form URL (Formspree, Web3Forms, Basin). data-netlify="true" is inert on Pages, and with `endpoint: ''` the form currently falls back to posting at /thanks/ — the visitor sees a success page and the enquiry vanishes. Do not "widen the CSP": the CSP lives only in netlify.toml, which Pages ignores. Pages serves no custom headers, so the move also silently drops CSP, HSTS, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options, Permissions-Policy and the immutable asset caching. A <meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy"> in Base.astro can restore script-src/form-action, but frame-ancestors and HSTS cannot be set from a meta tag at all.

4) Rebuild the redirects. public/_redirects is Netlify-only and is ignored by Pages; its 65 rules would have to be reissued as build-time meta-refresh + rel=canonical stub pages at each legacy path. This is a downgrade — a meta refresh is not a 301 and passes ranking signals weakly — and the wildcard rules (/pricing-plans/*, /service-page/*) cannot be expressed as stubs at all, so those legacy URLs would 404.

Worth saying plainly: this repo is already configured for Netlify (netlify.toml with the full header set, public/_redirects with real 301s). Netlify or Cloudflare Pages needs none of the four changes above and keeps the 301s and security headers. GitHub Pages is a genuine downgrade, not a lateral move.

claim: (a) CONFIRMED — GitHub Pages has no server-side redirect configuration; a Netlify _redirects file is ignored and served as a plain text file.
detail: Verified live against the existing preview deploy today (2026-09-23): `curl https://andy-arrow.github.io/pianotuningscy/_redirects` returns HTTP 200 with the file's raw contents (it is treated as a static asset, not as config), and `curl -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' https://andy-arrow.github.io/pianotuningscy/blank-1` returns 404 with an empty redirect_url — no 301 is issued. GitHub's docs describe Pages only as 'a static site hosting service that takes HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files straight from a repository' and state verbatim: 'GitHub Pages does not support server-side languages such as PHP, Ruby, or Python.' The only documented server-side behaviours are (1) the automatic www→apex redirect for a correctly configured custom domain, (2) HTTP→HTTPS when Enforce HTTPS is on, and (3) a custom 404 page via 404.html. No documented mechanism exists for per-path 301s. To re-verify at any time: `curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{redirect_url}\n' https://<site>/<legacy-path>`.

claim: The repo's legacy-URL map contains 45 active 301 rules and GitHub Pages would drop every one of them.
detail: `grep -vE '^\s*#|^\s*$' public/_redirects | wc -l` = 45 active rules in /Users/andy_aroditis/Library/Mobile Documents/com~apple~CloudDocs/CURSOR 2026/PIano Tunings CY/public/_redirects, covering /blank-1../blank-4, /book-online, /pricing-plans/*, /paywall, /plans, /service-page/* (5 named + wildcard), /booking-calendar/* and the Greek equivalents. On GitHub Pages every one of those legacy Wix URLs returns a 404 instead of a 301. Stated plainly: yes, GitHub Pages would silently discard the entire 14-year legacy-URL redirect map. The only Pages-compatible substitute is generating a real HTML file at each legacy path containing a <meta http-equiv="refresh"> plus <link rel="canonical">, which is a client-side redirect, not a 301, does not pass full link equity, and cannot express the wildcard rules (/service-page/*, /pricing-plans/*, /booking-calendar/*) or preserve query strings such as /book/?service=piano-tuning.

claim: (b) CONFIRMED — GitHub Pages allows no custom response headers; the CSP, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy and Permissions-Policy in netlify.toml cannot be applied.
detail: Live header dump of the Pages preview today returns only: server, content-type, last-modified, access-control-allow-origin: *, strict-transport-security: max-age=31556952, etag, expires, cache-control: max-age=600, plus Fastly/GitHub diagnostic headers. Absent: content-security-policy, referrer-policy, permissions-policy, x-content-type-options, x-frame-options. There is no documented _headers, netlify.toml, .htaccess or JSON equivalent in the GitHub Pages docs — the docs contain no header-configuration feature at all, and GitHub staff/community answers say headers are not configurable. Note one partial: HSTS IS already sent by GitHub (max-age=31556952 ≈ 1 year), but without includeSubDomains or preload, so it is weaker than the repo's max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload. CSP could only be partially reproduced via a <meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy"> tag, and the meta form ignores frame-ancestors (so clickjacking protection is lost entirely, since X-Frame-Options also cannot be set). Re-verify with: `curl -sSI https://<site>/ | grep -iE 'content-security|referrer|permissions|x-frame|x-content-type'`.

claim: The immutable caching rule for /_astro/* is also lost — GitHub Pages serves everything with a fixed cache-control: max-age=600.
detail: Observed header on the preview: `cache-control: max-age=600` (10 minutes) with `expires` 10 minutes ahead. netlify.toml asks for `public, max-age=31536000, immutable` on /_astro/* and `public, max-age=604800` on /og/*. Neither can be set on Pages. Practical effect: fingerprinted Astro bundles and OG images are re-validated every 10 minutes instead of cached for a year — slower repeat visits and worse Core Web Vitals, though not a correctness break.

claim: (c) CONFIRMED — GitHub Pages has no form handling; the data-netlify="true" contact form would break outright, and POST is rejected at the edge.
detail: Verified today: `curl -X POST https://andy-arrow.github.io/pianotuningscy/contact/` returns HTTP 405 Method Not Allowed. GitHub Pages serves GET/HEAD for static files only; the docs contain no form, function or backend feature. GitHub also explicitly prohibits using Pages for 'sensitive transactions like sending passwords or credit card numbers' and as 'a free web-hosting service to run your online business, e-commerce site, or any other website that is primarily directed at either facilitating commercial transactions'. On Pages the contact form would need a third-party endpoint (Formspree, Basin, Web3Forms, a Cloudflare Worker) or to be replaced by a mailto:/WhatsApp link — and the form-action 'self' in the repo's CSP would need changing to match.

claim: GitHub Pages usage limits are compatible with this 52-page site, but the prohibited-uses clause is a judgement call for a commercial business site.
detail: Documented limits: source repos have 'a recommended limit of 1 GB'; published sites 'may be no larger than 1 GB'; 'a soft bandwidth limit of 100 GB per month'; 'a soft limit of 10 builds per hour'. A 52-page Astro site is far inside all of these. The friction is policy, not capacity: Pages 'is not intended for or allowed to be used as a free web-hosting service to run your online business, e-commerce site, or any other website that is primarily directed at either facilitating commercial transactions'. A brochure site for a piano-tuning business with a booking form sits in a grey zone — there is no payment processing, but it is a commercial business site. That is an additional, non-technical reason not to make GitHub Pages the production host.

claim: Record types you can create/edit under Personal DNS settings: A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT, SRV, CAA, DS, NS, TLSA, SSHFP, plus the two pseudo-records Web forward and Web alias, plus a separate Name servers tab.
detail: Under DNS settings in the one.com Control Panel (Advanced settings tile → DNS settings → DNS records → "Create new record"), the "Personal DNS Settings" section lets you create exactly these, in the order the doc lists them: Web forward, Web alias, A, AAAA, CAA, CNAME, DS, MX, NS, TXT, SRV, TLSA, SSHFP, and Name servers. There is no ALIAS/ANAME type and no PTR option here — SPF and DMARC are both made as TXT records (DMARC on hostname _dmarc). Fields: Hostname is left empty for the domain root; an @ typed there is disregarded and treated as empty. The target field is labelled "IP address" for A and AAAA (not "Will point to", which was the old panel's wording), "Is an alias of" for CNAME, the mail server plus a Priority for MX, and "Value" for TXT. TTL is optional on every type — leave it empty for the 3600-second (1 hour) default; the allowed range is 600 to 86400. Creating a record that conflicts with a Standard DNS setting automatically disables that standard record, and "Reset DNS records" reverts everything to the standard settings. Because one.com is mid-rollout of a redesigned Control Panel, on-screen labels may not match the help-centre screenshots exactly — match fields by meaning, and before changing anything, screenshot the existing records so the current MX and TXT/SPF/DMARC values for the business email can be restored verbatim if needed.

claim: one.com does NOT support ALIAS, ANAME or CNAME flattening at the apex. The apex must be an A (or AAAA) record, so the Netlify/host apex target has to be an IP address.
detail:
one.com does not support ALIAS, ANAME or CNAME flattening. Its creatable record types are Web forward, Web alias, A, AAAA, CAA, CNAME, DS, MX, NS, TXT, SRV, TLSA, SSHFP and Name servers, and its CNAME guide states the Hostname field is "The subdomain (required)", so no CNAME can exist on the root. The apex must therefore be an A record pointing at an IP.

For Netlify: at the apex, create an A record with the Hostname field left empty (one.com's glossary: leave it empty for the domain root; a typed "@" is disregarded and treated as empty) pointing to 75.2.60.5. Use A, not AAAA — Netlify publishes no IPv6 apex address, so an AAAA record has no valid target here. If the site is on Netlify's High-Performance Edge, use the load-balancer IP shown in Netlify's "Pending DNS verification" details instead of 75.2.60.5.

For www: create a CNAME with Hostname "www" pointing at the site's <site-name>.netlify.app subdomain (Netlify's preferred routing; the apex A record cannot use the CDN's direct DNS routing).

Do not use Web alias or Web forward for pianotuningscy.com -> www; let Netlify perform the apex/www redirect. one.com itself documents that Web alias "isn't a real DNS record but a setting that mimics DNS behaviour", that it "won't work on a mobile device", that it "has a negative impact on SEO ranking", and that it is HTTP-only on Domain only or Email Essential plans.

Email safety: this change touches only the apex A record and the www CNAME. Do not modify or delete the MX records, the mail-related TXT/SPF/DKIM/DMARC records, or the autoconfig/mail CNAMEs — business email keeps working as long as those are left alone. Note that one.com automatically disables the conflicting entries under "Standard DNS settings" when a personal record collides with them; that applies to the web records you are replacing, not to mail.

claim: Because there is no apex ALIAS, the Netlify cutover uses Netlify's documented A-record fallback at the apex and a CNAME for www — but read the exact values off the Netlify UI rather than trusting a remembered IP.
detail: Netlify's documented external-DNS setup, in the order the doc gives it: first check one.com's record-type dropdown for ALIAS, ANAME, or flattened/virtual CNAME — if any is offered, use it on the apex (host empty or '@') pointing to apex-loadbalancer.netlify.com, which is Netlify's preferred option. Only if none is available, fall back to an A record on the apex (host empty or '@') pointing to 75.2.60.5. Either way, add a CNAME on host 'www' pointing to <site-name>.netlify.app. Before typing anything, open the Netlify UI at Domain management > Production domains and click "Pending DNS verification" next to the custom domain, and read the values from that modal — High-Performance Edge sites are given a different load balancer address there, and the modal is authoritative over any remembered IP. Netlify also recommends making www the primary domain and redirecting the apex to it, because an apex on external DNS cannot use Netlify's direct DNS routing. Change only the apex A/ALIAS and the www CNAME; leave the MX records and any SPF/DKIM/DMARC TXT records for the business email untouched, since those are independent of the web records. Allow up to 24 hours for propagation.

claim: Exact click-path to change the existing apex A record (currently 185.230.63.107, Wix): edit it in place, do not delete and recreate.
detail: Log in to the one.com Control Panel. Click "DNS settings" on the Advanced settings tile (in the redesigned panel the DNS settings entry point is in the bottom-right corner of the start page — one.com has not documented DNS moving into the left menu, so do not hunt for a "Domains" menu item; if you cannot find it, use the "Try new look" toggle in the bottom-left corner to switch back to the old design, where the Advanced settings tile is present). Click the "DNS records" tab. Scroll down to "Personal DNS settings" and, if the list looks incomplete, click "Show all". Find the A record whose Hostname is blank (the domain root) and whose value is 185.230.63.107. Click that row — it opens as an editable form, the same in-place edit one.com documents for TXT records ("Click the TXT record to edit it (do not delete it)"). Replace the value in the field labelled "IP address" — not "Will point to", which is not a one.com label — with the new IP (e.g. 75.2.60.5). Set TTL to 600 (one.com's documented minimum, 10 minutes) for a fast rollback window. Click "Update record". Do not click "Create record", and do not click "Delete record", the destructive button beside it; also avoid "Reset DNS records", which wipes all your personal records and reverts to one.com's standard settings. Two things the original instruction does not cover but that matter here: first, your business email is carried by the MX and TXT/SPF rows, not the A record, so editing only the apex A record leaves email untouched — do not modify any MX or TXT row while you are in this screen. Second, a Wix setup almost always has a companion record for www (typically a CNAME for host "www" pointing to www.wixdns.net, or a second A record); if you change only the apex, www.pianotuningscy.com will still resolve to Wix, so check for that row and repoint it to the new host in the same visit.

claim: Exact click-path to change the existing www CNAME (currently www43.wixdns.net): same screen, click the CNAME row under Personal DNS settings and edit 'Is an alias of'.
detail:
Change the existing www CNAME in place — no delete needed in the normal case.

1. Log in to the one.com Control Panel. Open DNS settings. On the old design this is the "Advanced settings" tile; on the new design (there is a "Try new look" toggle bottom-left) use the left-hand menu instead — one.com is mid-rollout and every DNS help article now carries a banner saying the old tile step may not match your screen.
2. Click "DNS records".
3. Scroll down to "Personal DNS settings". If you do not see the existing records listed, click "Show all" — the list can be collapsed, and this is the usual reason a row seems not to be editable.
4. Click the CNAME row with Hostname "www" to open it for editing.
5. Change "Is an alias of" from www43.wixdns.net to your Netlify subdomain, e.g. pianotuningscy.netlify.app. No trailing dot is needed. It must be a hostname, not an IP address — one.com rejects an IP in this field.
6. Set TTL to 600. That is one.com's documented minimum (default 3600, maximum 86400).
7. Click "Update record".

Fallback only if your panel genuinely will not open the row: click "Delete record", then under "create new record" click "CNAME" and enter Hostname "www", "Is an alias of" = your Netlify subdomain, TTL 600, then "Create record". Re-create immediately; there will be a short gap during which www does not resolve.

Two things to know before you type: this edit touches only the www hostname, so your MX records and business email are not affected. And it does not move the bare/apex domain — if the apex currently points at Wix, it will keep serving Wix until you change that record separately.

Sources: editing an existing record and the "Update record" button, plus the "Show all" step, are documented at https://help.one.com/hc/en-us/articles/10311693187985-How-to-edit-SPF-records-to-enable-Exchange ; the "Is an alias of" field and the no-IP rule at https://help.one.com/hc/en-us/articles/360000803517-How-do-I-create-a-CNAME-record ; Personal DNS settings and the TTL range at https://help.one.com/hc/en-us/articles/115005595925-Manage-your-DNS-settings ; the Control Panel redesign at https://help.one.com/hc/en-us/articles/45610357369361-Navigating-the-new-one-com-Control-Panel-design

claim: one.com auto-creates 'Standard DNS settings' for the hosting it sells you, and a conflicting personal record automatically disables the matching standard one — there is no 'disable web hosting first' switch to find.
detail: one.com auto-creates "Standard DNS settings" when your web space is set up, and a conflicting personal record disables the standard setting automatically — there is no "disable web hosting first" switch to find. Official wording (help.one.com article 115005595925, "Manage your DNS settings", last updated 20 Sep 2026): "When your web space is set up, we create some standard DNS settings for you to make your domain work. You can find them under Standard DNS settings." and "When you create conflicting records, the standard DNS settings will automatically be disabled. Click Reset DNS records to remove your personal settings, and change everything back to the standard settings." That is why the current Wix A/CNAME records work without you having cancelled one.com hosting, and it is why one.com's own guides for connecting a domain to an external site builder (e.g. Squarespace) tell you only to create the A/CNAME records under DNS settings > DNS records, with no step to cancel or disable hosting first. Two things the docs do NOT state, so treat them as observations of your own panel rather than documented behaviour: (a) the per-entry on/off sliders under Standard DNS settings > "Show all" (green = active, grey = disabled) and the claim that the first six entries are the A/AAAA records for domain.com, *.domain.com and www.domain.com are not described in any one.com help article, and one.com is currently rolling out a new Control Panel design that several of its own guides warn may not match existing screenshots — so look at what your panel actually shows before relying on that ordering; (b) the doc says "the standard DNS settings will automatically be disabled", not "the matching standard one", so do not assume from the wording alone that only the one conflicting row is affected. You still do not need to touch those toggles for this cutover — creating the personal A/CNAME on the same hostname is enough. Because business email runs on this domain, after you save the new records reload DNS settings and confirm your MX rows (and any mail-related TXT/SPF rows) are still present and active before you walk away, and do NOT click "Reset DNS records", which wipes your personal records and reverts everything to one.com's standard settings.

claim: The one destructive control on that page is 'Reset DNS records' — it deletes every personal record at once and restores one.com's standard set. Never click it during the cutover.
detail:
The destructive control to avoid is "Reset DNS records", at the bottom of DNS Records in the one.com control panel (Advanced Settings > DNS settings). one.com documents it as: "Click Reset DNS records to remove your personal settings, and change everything back to the standard settings." [Manage your DNS settings, https://help.one.com/hc/en-us/articles/115005595925-Manage-your-DNS-settings]

Effect during a cutover: every record you added by hand is removed at once and one.com's defaults come back. That means your new apex A record and www CNAME vanish and the domain falls back to one.com's own webspace (old or parked content) — but the more serious loss is any custom MX record. If mail runs on Google Workspace, Microsoft 365 or anything other than one.com, Reset restores one.com's MX and mail stops arriving at your provider with no bounce to warn you. Custom TXT records (SPF, DKIM, DMARC, domain-verification) go the same way. No undo is documented. Do not click it at any point during the migration.

Two corrections to the usual framing of this warning:

1. It is not the only destructive control on the page. Each personal record has its own delete (trash) icon, and the Standard DNS settings sliders carry one.com's own data-loss warning — from the unpublish guide: "If you deactivate more than just the first six settings, you might also deactivate other services, like, for example, emails and FTP access. You risk losing new emails, so please follow our instructions closely." [https://help.one.com/hc/en-us/articles/360011299917-How-can-I-temporarily-unpublish-my-website] Unlike Reset, the sliders are documented as reversible: click them green again, ~90 minutes to propagate.

2. You should not touch those sliders during the cutover at all. one.com states: "When you create conflicting records, the standard DNS settings will automatically be disabled." Adding your own apex A record automatically disables one.com's standard A/AAAA records for that host. Add the new records; leave Standard DNS settings alone.

Before you change anything, screenshot or copy out the full current record list — especially every MX and TXT row — so it can be retyped if something goes wrong.

claim: Editing the apex A and www CNAME does not touch the MX records or ftp — those are one.com-managed standard records on different names/types, and live DNS confirms the split.
detail:
Editing the apex A record and the www CNAME does not touch MX or ftp. DNS records are keyed by name + type, so an A on the root cannot disable an MX on the root, and a CNAME on 'www' cannot affect a CNAME on 'ftp'. one.com's own rule — "When you create conflicting records, the standard DNS settings will automatically be disabled" — applies only per name+type, and for the apex A and www it has already fired: both are personal records today (apex A 185.230.63.107, www CNAME www43.wixdns.net), so re-editing them changes nothing about MX or ftp.

Two things on that same screen genuinely will break you, and neither is the edit itself:
1. Do NOT click "Reset DNS records". The doc says it removes your personal settings and reverts everything to one.com's standard settings — that would delete the Wix apex A and www CNAME and take the site down.
2. Do NOT change the name servers. They must stay ns01.one.com and ns02.one.com. Moving them (including accepting Wix's "connect via nameservers" option instead of pointing records) hands the whole zone elsewhere and kills the mail with it.

Open only the two rows you intend to change. Do not touch the "Standard DNS settings" block — that is where the one.com-managed MX and ftp rows live; identify rows by that section, not by TTL (one.com's TTLs are default 3600, minimum 600, maximum 86400, and the MX set sits at 10800, so TTL alone does not tell you which rows are hand-made).

After the edit, verify against the authoritative nameserver, not a cache — the MX TTL is 10800 (3 hours), so a cached lookup can return the old, correct-looking MX set and falsely reassure you:

  dig +short @ns01.one.com pianotuningscy.com MX
  dig +short @ns01.one.com pianotuningscy.com A
  dig +short @ns01.one.com www.pianotuningscy.com CNAME
  dig +short @ns01.one.com ftp.pianotuningscy.com CNAME

The MX line must still read: 10 mx1.mailpod15-cph3.g1i.one.com. (and mx2, mx3, mx4). If it is empty or different, stop and restore it before doing anything else.

claim: TTL control: the field is optional per record, minimum 600s, default 3600s if left blank, maximum 86400s. You cannot pre-lower TTL below 10 minutes for the cutover.
detail: TTL control: the field is optional on each record. one.com's documented limits are minimum 600 seconds (10 minutes), maximum 86400 seconds (24 hours), and default 3600 seconds (1 hour) when the field is left blank. You therefore cannot pre-lower TTL below 10 minutes for the cutover — 600 is the floor. Important: "blank" does not mean "keep the current value" — it means 3600, so on any record you create or re-create during the switch, type 600 in explicitly rather than leaving the field empty, or that record will silently carry a 1-hour TTL. Verify in the DNS panel that the apex and www records currently show 600 before assuming no pre-lowering is needed; that is a property of your zone, not a default. Separately from TTL, one.com's own guides state that a DNS change "can take up to 90 minutes before the DNS change is active" (and for DKIM CNAME records, "usually takes up to 240 minutes ... to propagate across the internet; it will not work immediately"). Plan the switch for a quiet window and expect a mixed-serving period where some resolvers return the old target and some the new, rather than an instant flip.

claim: Do not change nameservers for this cutover — one.com says that kills the hosting-bundled services, and business email is the thing you cannot afford to break.
detail: Do not change the nameservers for this cutover. one.com's own documentation states that "when you change the name servers for your domain to those of a third party, all features included with your web hosting subscription will stop working - for example, the Website Builder, Online shop and email," and recommends the alternative directly: "If you want to connect to an external service, it's often possible to achieve the same result by changing your DNS settings." Since the mailboxes are on the one.com web hosting subscription, delegating the zone would take business email down, not just the site. Instead, leave ns01.one.com / ns02.one.com in place and edit only the individual records the new host requires (the A/ALIAS or CNAME for the site) in one.com's DNS settings, leaving MX, SPF, DKIM and any autodiscover records untouched. If the nameservers have already been moved at any point, restoring mail is not a matter of putting back a single record: it requires re-creating the MX as cluster.mx.service.one — the "cluster" part is specific to your domain and only one.com support can tell you which one it is, and on domains not yet migrated to the new platform the format is still domain.tld.mx.one.com — plus deleting every other MX record, adding the SPF TXT record v=spf1 include:_custspf.one.com ~all (merged into any existing SPF record, never as a second one), and adding four DKIM CNAME records whose values must also be requested from one.com support. Verify both help.one.com articles in a browser immediately before making changes, and allow up to 24 hours for propagation.

claim: Deleting the Wix records instead of editing them can re-expose one.com's standard A records, serving old one.com hosting content on the domain until the new record exists.
detail: Deleting the Wix records instead of editing them can re-expose one.com's standard A/AAAA records, potentially serving old one.com hosting content on the domain. one.com documents that "When you create conflicting records, the standard DNS settings will automatically be disabled" — the six affected standard entries are the A and AAAA records for pianotuningscy.com, *.pianotuningscy.com and www.pianotuningscy.com. one.com does NOT document the reverse direction, so do not assume the standard records silently return the instant you delete the personal record; the documented ways back to standard are the "Reset DNS records" button or clicking the sliders green manually, and one.com states that reactivating standard settings takes 90 minutes to take effect. Practical guidance: edit each record in place rather than deleting it, using whatever edit control your panel shows (one.com's docs only name a "Create record" button, and the Control Panel is mid-redesign, so the edit control's label may differ from what older guides show). If you must delete, create the replacement in the same session. Afterwards, verify visually: go to DNS settings > DNS records > scroll to Standard DNS settings > Show all, and confirm the six apex/wildcard/www A and AAAA entries are still grey, not green. Note that one.com's default TTL is 3600 seconds, so resolvers may keep serving the previous value for up to an hour regardless of what the panel shows.

claim: There is currently no SPF and no DMARC on the domain; once the site move is done, both can be enabled with one toggle each in the same DNS screen, because mail stays at one.com.
detail:
After the web cutover has settled — and only while the domain's nameservers are still ns01/ns02.one.com, which they are today — enable both standard records in the one.com Control Panel, one at a time:

SPF: Control Panel > Domains > DNS settings > scroll to Standard DNS settings > find "TXT domain.com" (directly above "TXT _dmarc.domain.com") > enable its toggle.

DMARC: same screen — Domains > DNS settings > DNS records > under Standard DNS settings choose "Show all" if the list is collapsed > find "TXT _dmarc.domain.com" > enable its toggle.

Each can take up to 90 minutes to become active; verify with `dig +short TXT pianotuningscy.com` and `dig +short TXT _dmarc.pianotuningscy.com` before moving on. one.com is rolling out a redesigned Control Panel, so labels may not match the screenshots exactly.

Important condition: this only works if the site move keeps one.com as the DNS host (i.e. you point A/ALIAS/CNAME records at Netlify from inside the one.com DNS panel). If the domain is instead delegated to Netlify's nameservers, these toggles have no effect — SPF and DMARC would then have to be added manually as TXT records at Netlify, and one.com's automatic DKIM signing would need extra setup from their support.

Netlify form notifications are sent from Netlify's own domain and need no SPF change on pianotuningscy.com.

claim: DNS editing lives in one place, but the click path differs between one.com's old and new Control Panel designs — check which one you are on before following any guide.
detail: Old design: log in to the one.com Control Panel, scroll to the 'Advanced settings' tile, click 'DNS settings', then the 'DNS records' tab at the top. New design (rolled out 2026, articles updated Sept 2026 use it): left-hand menu 'Domains' > 'DNS settings' > 'DNS records'. During the transition a 'Try new look' toggle sits in the bottom-left corner and switches between designs. The DNS records screen itself is the same in both: 'Create new record' buttons at the top (one per record type), then 'Personal DNS settings' (your records), then 'Standard DNS settings' with a 'Show all' link.

claim: The zone is DNSSEC-signed by one.com (DS at the registry, algorithm 13). Editing A/CNAME records inside the panel is re-signed automatically and is safe; switching nameservers away is where DNSSEC bites.
detail: Verified today: DS 60405 13 2 f038363d... present at the parent, DNSKEY algorithm 13, resolvers return AD=1. one.com: 'DNSSEC is enabled and activated by default when using one.com's name servers' and 'DNSSEC is automatically disabled if you change to external name servers.' So if you ever moved DNS to Netlify DNS or Cloudflare, do it through the Control Panel's DNS settings > Name servers tab so the DS is handled, otherwise every validating resolver returns SERVFAIL and the domain goes dark. Keeping NS at ns01/ns02.one.com avoids the issue entirely.

claim: The domain sits on one.com's new hosting platform, which changes two things you may hit later: subdomains are created in the panel, and one.com's own platform migrations can change your server IP/DNS underneath you.
detail: Fingerprints: ftp.pianotuningscy.com -> ftp.c3ub80nh5.service.one and MX on mailpod15-cph3.g1i.one.com, both new-platform formats. On the new platform, subdomains are added under Advanced settings > Subdomains (not by creating a folder in File Manager). one.com's own Cloudflare FAQ warns: 'During migrations, we may move your domain to a different server, which can cause changes to your IP and DNS settings' — a reason to re-check the apex A after any one.com migration email, since your apex will then be pointing at Netlify and must not be silently reset.

claim: No CAA record exists, so Let's Encrypt/Netlify certificate issuance is unblocked — and if you ever add one in the panel, you must include the new host's CA.
detail: Verified today: CAA query returns no records, so any CA may issue. one.com does support creating CAA records (DNS records > CAA, 'Value' is the three-space-separated parts, e.g. 0 issue "letsencrypt.org"). Leave CAA absent for the cutover; adding a restrictive one before Netlify provisions its certificate would cause issuance to fail.

claim: On a legacy plan the meter counts verified submissions only, and behaviour at the cap differs between free and paid
detail:
On a legacy plan the Forms meter counts verified submissions only — Akismet-flagged spam lands in the separate Spam submissions list and honeypot/reCAPTCHA-2 rejections are discarded entirely, so neither consumes quota. Behaviour at the cap differs sharply by plan:

- Paid legacy plans: "When usage reaches a level limit, the site will automatically upgrade to the next level or package." It costs money; nothing breaks.
- Free legacy tier: the cap is Forms Level 0, "100 form submissions per month and 10 MB of uploaded files per month". Hitting 100% does NOT merely refuse further submissions — per the Billing FAQ for legacy plans, "when reaching 100% of the limit, new builds will be disabled and all sites on your account will be paused." The site goes offline, as do any other sites on the same team. Warning emails arrive at 50%, 75%, 90% and 100%.

Values are right; tighten the wording before it is typed into the panel:

1. Hostname field, not "@". one.com's DNS records table does not use "@" for the root. Per one.com's own help, you leave the hostname/name field EMPTY (or it shows the bare domain) for the apex. 2. Edit the existing record rather than delete-then-add. Use the A value and the .netlify.app hostname that modal shows for YOUR site. 75.2.60.5 is the documented default; a High-Performance Edge site is given a different load balancer and a dedicated subdomain instead of <site>.netlify.app.

4. Email is untouched by this change — worth saying plainly to the owner. MX records are a separate record type; changing the apex A and the www CNAME does not move mail. Leave the MX records, any SPF/DKIM/DMARC TXT records, mail.pianotuningscy.com (A 46.30.211.122) and ftp.pianotuningscy.com (CNAME ftp.c3ub80nh5.service.one) exactly as they are. Do not use one.com's "restore default DNS settings" / reset button, and do not change nameservers — either would take the mail down.

5. Set expectations on timing. Netlify's doc says propagation can take several hours and up to 24 hours. Lower the TTL on the two records to the minimum one.com allows a few hours BEFORE the cutover if you want a fast rollback. Rollback is: apex A back to 185.230.63.107, www CNAME back to www43.wixdns.net.

6. Netlify's own recommendation, for the record: because an apex A record cannot use their global CDN routing the way a CNAME can, Netlify recommends making the www subdomain the primary domain and redirecting the apex to it. Configure that in Netlify's domain settings; it does not change the two DNS records above.

claim: MX is completely independent of A and CNAME. Changing the web records cannot affect mail routing or deliverability, provided you edit individual records and never change nameservers or put a CNAME at the apex.
detail:
Mail routing for pianotuningscy.com is driven entirely by the MX RRset (mx1–mx4.mailpod15-cph3.g1i.one.com, all preference 10). Per RFC 5321 §5.1, once one or more MX records exist for a name, sending mail servers MUST NOT use that name's A/AAAA records for delivery. So editing the apex A record and the www CNAME to point at Netlify cannot reroute mail, and your one.com mailboxes are untouched.

Three things to avoid, all of which would break mail:
(a) Do not change the nameservers away from ns01.one.com / ns02.one.com, and do not use any "import zone", "replace zone" or "reset DNS to default" function. Edit records one at a time.
(b) Do not put a CNAME at the apex (host @ or blank). A CNAME forbids any other record at the same name (RFC 1034 §3.6.2, RFC 2181 §10.1), which would destroy the MX set — and the apex must carry SOA and NS anyway. One.com does not support ALIAS/ANAME, so the apex must be an A record.
(c) Do not delete TXT records or mail-related subdomain records (mail, autoconfig, autodiscover, *._domainkey) while tidying up.

Exact values, from Netlify's current external-DNS documentation:
- Apex: A record, host @, value 75.2.60.5
- www: CNAME, host www, value <your-site>.netlify.app (this replaces the existing www43.wixdns.net CNAME)

One correction to the deliverability note: the A record change is irrelevant to deliverability only if your new SPF record does not use the a or mx mechanisms. If it did, the Netlify IP would become an authorized sender for your domain. Use one.com's documented include-only form:
- TXT, host @, value: v=spf1 include:_custspf.one.com ~all
Publish exactly one SPF TXT record at the apex — a second one invalidates both.
- TXT, host _dmarc, value: v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:you@pianotuningscy.com
Start at p=none and only tighten to quarantine/reject after the reports confirm your legitimate senders pass.

Source correction: the routing rule comes from RFC 5321 §5.1, not RFC 1034 — RFC 1034 defers the MX lookup algorithm to RFC 974. RFC 1034 §3.6.2 is the right citation only for the CNAME restriction.

Reasons to hold, in order:
(1) Rollback. Until the Netlify certificate is issued, the redirects are verified and the form has produced a real submission, your only recovery is re-pointing the domain back at Wix — and that only works while the Wix site still answers for that domain. (3) Any Wix-side booking or contact data still needs exporting.

Unpublishing and hiding from search are separate, explicit actions. Skipping this leaves a duplicate of your content indexed under a wixsite.com URL competing with the new site.

Your domain is registered and DNS-hosted at one.com, not Wix, and Wix documents that "your site plan and domain name are separate services and therefore need to be canceled separately" — so ending the Wix plan carries no risk to the domain. claim: Add this SPF record while you are in the one.com DNS panel: host @ (blank), type TXT, value: v=spf1 include:_custspf.one.com ~all
detail:
Before typing anything, check whether one.com is already publishing an SPF record for you. In the one.com Control Panel go to Domains > DNS settings and scroll to "Standard DNS settings", then look for the entry "TXT domain.com" (it sits directly above "TXT _dmarc.domain.com"). Also run a check from outside the panel: `dig +short TXT yourdomain.com` — the standard record is published by the toggle and does not appear in the custom "DNS records" list, so an empty DNS records list does not mean you have no SPF.

Then pick one of two paths, never both:

(a) If the "TXT domain.com" toggle exists — just switch it on. That is what one.com now documents for domains on one.com nameservers, and it publishes their standard SPF for you. Do not also add a TXT record by hand; two SPF records at the apex is a permanent error under RFC 7208 and mail providers will ignore both.

(b) If that toggle is not there, or you already know you will be sending from another service (Mailchimp, a CRM, Google Workspace) and therefore need a record you control — turn the standard toggle OFF if it is on, then go to DNS settings > DNS records > create new record > TXT and enter: hostname left empty (blank = the apex), value `v=spf1 include:_custspf.one.com ~all`, TTL left empty (defaults to 3600). Click Create record.

Either way there must be exactly one SPF TXT at the apex when you are done — verify with `dig +short TXT yourdomain.com` and confirm only one string starts with "v=spf1". Allow up to 90 minutes for the change to go live. Keep ~all (softfail); only consider -all after a few weeks of clean DMARC aggregate reports. Any future sender gets its include added inside this same single record, never as a second record, and the total must stay under SPF's 10-DNS-lookup limit. Netlify Forms notifications are sent from Netlify's own domain, so they need no entry here. None of this touches MX or the A/CNAME records, so neither your email nor the site goes down from this step.

Note that the cited page (help.one.com article 115005595945) no longer documents the manual record — the verbatim value above now comes from one.com's external-nameservers guide (article 17038200070545) and its Exchange SPF guide (article 10311693187985). claim: Add this DMARC record: host _dmarc, type TXT, value: v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc@pianotuningscy.com; adkim=r; aspf=r
detail:
Add one DNS record in the one.com panel — Type: TXT, Host/Name: _dmarc (the panel appends the domain, giving _dmarc.pianotuningscy.com; if the panel wants the full name instead, enter _dmarc.pianotuningscy.com), TTL: default/3600. Value, as a single line with no line breaks and no surrounding quotes unless the panel requires them:

Do this first: create the mailbox dmarc@pianotuningscy.com in one.com (or change the rua address to a real mailbox you already read), otherwise the aggregate reports bounce. adkim=r and aspf=r are the RFC 9989 defaults, so they are optional — they only make the record self-documenting. Do not add pct=; RFC 9989 (May 2026, obsoletes RFC 7489) removed it, along with rf and ri.
