claim: Keep SPF/DMARC as a separate, earlier change from the web cutover — add them a few days before, not in the same sitting as the A/CNAME flip.
detail:
Yes — keep SPF/DMARC as a separate, earlier change from the web cutover. Both are TXT records and cannot affect web serving, so separating them means that if anything goes odd with mail you know which change caused it. Corrected sequence:

Day -3: Add SPF and DMARC. Write the SPF record for whoever will be sending mail AFTER the cutover, not just today's setup — if the new web host will send contact-form or order email from its own servers, include it now, or that mail starts failing SPF on day 0. Include an rua= address in the DMARC record or you get no reports at all: `v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:you@pianotuningscy.com`. Leave it at p=none through the whole migration; only consider quarantine/reject weeks later, after reading reports.

Same day, confirm the records: `dig +short TXT pianotuningscy.com` and `dig +short TXT _dmarc.pianotuningscy.com`. If either comes back empty or stale, re-run against the authoritative nameserver — `dig +short TXT pianotuningscy.com @<your-dns-provider's-nameserver>` — because the plain command answers from a cache. Then send a test mail from the domain's real mail system to a Gmail address and check Show original reads spf=pass and dmarc=pass.

Lower the A/CNAME TTLs to 300 at the same sitting as the SPF change (day -3), not day -1. A new low TTL only takes effect once the OLD cached TTL expires, so lowering it 24 hours ahead is only enough if the current TTL is 24 hours or less; Cloudflare's migration guidance is 24-48 hours ahead, or longer if your current TTL is longer. Check the current value first with `dig +noall +answer pianotuningscy.com A` and give it at least that long. Lowering TTL is harmless and reversible, so doing it early costs nothing.

Day 0: Flip the A and CNAME records. Leave the TTLs at 300 for a day or two after, until the new site is confirmed good, then raise them back to 3600.

claim: Post-cutover DNS/TLS checks: run these exact commands and expect these answers.
detail:
Post-cutover DNS/TLS checks.

DNS — query named resolvers rather than trusting your local one:

  dig +short A pianotuningscy.com @1.1.1.1
  dig +short A pianotuningscy.com @8.8.8.8

Expect 75.2.60.5 IF you created an apex A record (Netlify's documented fallback for providers that have no ALIAS/ANAME support — one.com is one of those, so this is the path you are on). If you instead used an ALIAS/ANAME/flattened CNAME to apex-loadbalancer.netlify.com — Netlify's recommended option where supported — expect whatever that hostname currently resolves to, not necessarily that literal IP. If the site is on High-Performance Edge, expect the dedicated IP shown in your Pending DNS verification modal instead. Either way, the old 185.230.63.107 must be gone.

  dig +short CNAME www.pianotuningscy.com @1.1.1.1

Expect <site>.netlify.app, and no www43.wixdns.net. If your provider flattens CNAMEs this may come back empty — in that case check `dig +short A www.pianotuningscy.com` instead and confirm it lands on Netlify.

Email — these must be UNCHANGED. Confirm all four, not just that "some MX exists":

  dig +short MX pianotuningscy.com @1.1.1.1

Expect mx1, mx2, mx3, mx4 .mailpod15-cph3.g1i.one.com. Then:

  dig +short TXT pianotuningscy.com @1.1.1.1
  dig +short TXT _dmarc.pianotuningscy.com @1.1.1.1

Note the first returns EVERY apex TXT record, so expect the SPF record among possibly others (site-verification strings etc.) — read it, don't just count lines. Also verify any DKIM selector records one.com uses, and any autodiscover/autoconfig records, survived the edit.

HTTP:

  curl -sI https://www.pianotuningscy.com/

Expect HTTP/2 200, `server: Netlify` (Netlify's own documented "is it us yet" check), and the netlify.toml headers: strict-transport-security, content-security-policy, x-content-type-options.

  curl -sI http://pianotuningscy.com/
  curl -sI https://pianotuningscy.com/

Expect a 301 toward https://www.pianotuningscy.com/. It may take two hops (http apex -> https apex -> https www); `curl -sIL` shows the whole chain. Do not expect the netlify.toml custom headers on the 301 responses — they appear on the final 200.

TLS — use this instead of the -subject form, which does not print the SAN list and which can show an empty subject on current Let's Encrypt certificates:

  openssl s_client -connect www.pianotuningscy.com:443 -servername www.pianotuningscy.com </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
    | openssl x509 -noout -issuer -dates -ext subjectAltName

Expect a Let's Encrypt issuer, valid dates, and a subjectAltName listing BOTH www.pianotuningscy.com and pianotuningscy.com. Repeat with -servername pianotuningscy.com.

If the cert covers only one of the two names, that is a known and expected state when DNS was still propagating at issuance time: wait for the old TTLs to expire, then click Renew certificate in Netlify. Check from outside your own network too (mobile data, or an online dig tool), since your local resolver may still be caching the old Wix answers.

claim: Verify the production build actually shed its preview flags: robots.txt, sitemap and canonicals are the three things that will silently keep the site out of Google if PREVIEW env vars leak into the Netlify build.
detail: Run these four checks against the Netlify deploy URL (https://<site>.netlify.app) BEFORE changing DNS — www.pianotuningscy.com still serves the old Wix site, so checking it now tests Wix, not the new build, and gives a misleading pass on robots.txt and a misleading fail on the sitemap. Then repeat all four on the real domain after propagation. (1) /robots.txt must be the production variant: "User-agent: *", "Allow: /", then "Disallow: /thanks/" and "Disallow: /el/efcharistoume/" (both expected and correct — not preview leakage), then "Sitemap: https://www.pianotuningscy.com/sitemap-index.xml". If it instead reads "# Review deployment — not the live site." with "Disallow: /", PUBLIC_PREVIEW=true has leaked into the Netlify build; fix the env var and redeploy before pointing DNS. (2) /sitemap-index.xml must return XML containing a <loc> for /sitemap-0.xml; an HTML page or a 404 means PREVIEW_SITE or PREVIEW_BASE was set at build time and the sitemap integration was skipped. (3) curl -s <url>/ | grep -i -E 'noindex|canonical|hreflang' must show no noindex, canonical https://www.pianotuningscy.com/ (with trailing slash), and hreflang en-CY, el-CY and x-default — note that on the Netlify preview URL the canonical will already read www.pianotuningscy.com, which is correct. (4) curl -s <url>/ | grep -c '/pianotuningscy/' must return 0. Also confirm in the Netlify UI (Site configuration > Environment variables) that PUBLIC_PREVIEW, PREVIEW_SITE and PREVIEW_BASE are absent — those belong only to the GitHub Pages preview workflow. Google's rule is unchanged and is why check (1) comes first: a page blocked by robots.txt never has its noindex read, so a stray Disallow: / can keep the site out of Search while every page still looks fine in a browser.

claim: In Google Search Console: submit the new sitemap, do NOT use the Change of Address tool, and re-verify the property if needed.
detail:
Google Search Console (do this after DNS has cut over and the new site is serving on the live domain):

1. Verify ownership. Prefer a Domain property (enter the bare domain, no https:// and no www). Google requires DNS verification for this type and it covers www, apex, http and https in one property — add the TXT record Google gives you in the same one.com DNS panel you are already in, alongside the A/CNAME changes. If you already have a URL-prefix property (e.g. https://www.example.com/) it keeps working; you only need to re-verify if the verification method breaks during the move (for example, an HTML file or meta tag that no longer exists on the new build).

2. Do NOT use the Change of Address tool. Google's site-move documentation states you only need it "when moving from one domain or subdomain to another," and that you don't need it "for HTTP to HTTPS moves, switching between www and non-www on the same domain, or moving paths within the same domain." It also cannot be used here: the tool runs from a domain-level property of the old domain you are leaving, and in this move there is no old domain.

3. Sitemaps > submit sitemap-index.xml. Then delete the old Wix sitemap entry — but note it is cosmetic: per Google, "Deleting a sitemap removes the sitemap from this report, but Google won't forget the sitemap or any URLs listed in it." What actually retires the old URLs is the 301 redirects, so verify every legacy Wix path returns 301 to its new equivalent before you worry about the sitemap entry.

4. URL Inspection > Test Live URL on the homepage, one EN service page, one EL page, and one redirected legacy URL. Confirm each reports "URL is available to Google" with no noindex and the correct canonical. Use "Request indexing" on the top handful of pages only — it has a limited daily quota and is a nudge, not a substitute for the sitemap.

5. Monitor for two to four weeks: the Pages report (formerly Index coverage) and Crawl stats. A spike in "Not found (404)" means a redirect gap; "Excluded by 'noindex' tag" means a leaked preview/staging noindex flag shipped to production. Also check Settings > Crawl stats for a rise in failed fetches right after the DNS change.

6. If the GitHub Pages preview was ever indexed, keep it noindexed or take the Pages deployment down once Netlify is live, so it cannot compete as a duplicate.

Separately, and more important than any of the above: if this domain carries business email, do not touch the MX records, or the SPF/DKIM/DMARC TXT records, while changing the A/CNAME records for the website. Write down the current MX and mail-related TXT values before you edit anything, and confirm they are byte-for-byte unchanged after you save.

claim: Post-cutover email verification: send and receive a real message the same day, and confirm SPF/DMARC pass in the headers.
detail:
Post-cutover email verification. Before you touch DNS, record the current MX, SPF, DKIM and DMARC records (dig MX example.com; dig TXT example.com) and send one test each way so you have a baseline. A web-hosting change should not alter MX or those TXT records at all.

Same day after the change, repeat the test: send from the business address to a Gmail address and to an Outlook.com address, and have someone reply from an external address to the business mailbox to confirm inbound delivery.

Reading the result: in Gmail, open the message, More > Show original, and check the SPF, DKIM and DMARC rows (you can also paste the headers into Google Admin Toolbox Messageheader). Outlook.com has no "Show original" — use View message source and read the Authentication-Results header (spf=pass; dkim=pass; dmarc=pass). Aim for all three passing, but note that under RFC 9989 (May 2026, which obsoletes RFC 7489) DMARC passes when SPF or DKIM produces an aligned pass — a single SPF fail with DKIM aligned is still dmarc=pass and is not by itself a reason to roll back.

Do not rely on a successful send as proof the records are right: DNS caching means your test may have used cached data. Confirm directly with dig MX example.com @8.8.8.8 and dig TXT example.com @8.8.8.8 and compare against the values you recorded.

DMARC reports: you only receive them if your DMARC record includes a rua= address. Google documents aggregate reports as "usually sent once a day"; RFC 9990 specifies daily or more frequent. Expect the first report from a large receiver within about 24 hours, but collect several days from several receivers before acting — a low-volume domain gets thin data. Stay at p=none until the reports show all your legitimate mail authenticating, then move to p=quarantine. Note that RFC 9989 removed the pct tag, so a percentage-based ramp is no longer available; the path is none, then quarantine, then reject.

Sources: RFC 9989 and RFC 9990 (DMARC and DMARC aggregate reporting, May 2026), RFC 7208 (SPF, still current), Google Workspace Help "About DMARC reports" and "Set up DMARC".

claim: Content and functionality pass after the flip: check both languages, the form end to end, and analytics.
detail:
Content and functionality pass after the flip: check both languages, the form end to end, and analytics.

Before testing the form, confirm two Netlify settings that are NOT on by default and that no amount of correct markup substitutes for:
- Forms > Enable form detection must be turned on, and it only takes effect starting with the next site deploy. If it was enabled after the last deploy, trigger a redeploy first, otherwise the POST returns 404 and no submission is ever recorded.
- Forms > Submission notifications must have an email notification added. Netlify does not email you on submission by default.

Then verify:
- Walk the EN and EL homepage, services, booking and contact pages on the real domain; confirm the language switcher produces /el/... URLs (e.g. /el/epikoinonia/) with correct Greek chrome — re-verify now that the base path is gone, since a prior commit fixed Greek pages serving English chrome under a base path.
- Submit the contact form from the live domain in both languages and confirm each submission appears under the "enquiry" form in Netlify Forms and that the notification email arrives. Both pages use the same form name, so submissions merge into one form; that is expected.
- Confirm the honeypot field (name="company-website") is still present in the delivered HTML but visually hidden via CSS — it must not be removed or disabled, and its name must be included in the POST body (it is, because the handler encodes FormData).
- Confirm images/OG images load: curl -sI on an /og/ file returns 200 with Cache-Control: public, max-age=604800 (7 days).
- Test on a phone.
- Watch the browser console on each template for CSP violations; netlify.toml allows only 'self' and plausible.io for connect-src/script-src, and the form's AJAX POST goes to '/' (same origin), so it is covered by connect-src 'self' and form-action 'self'.
- Confirm Plausible is recording pageviews and the "Enquiry sent" event for pianotuningscy.com.

claim: Rollback plan, written down before you start: revert two records.
detail:
Rollback plan, written down before you start.

STEP 0 — do this before changing anything. Open the one.com DNS panel and screenshot (or export) the full record list. The rollback values are whatever that screenshot shows, not what any documentation says. Do not rely on memory or on a value from a Wix help page: the www CNAME under the pointing method is account-specific in its legacy wwwNN.wixdns.net form, and Wix's current published generic value is pointing.wixdns.net, so a doc lookup can hand you the wrong target. Write the two lines out by hand from the screenshot:
  A    @     <exact current value, expected 185.230.63.107>   TTL 300
  CNAME www <exact current value, e.g. www43.wixdns.net>      TTL 300

TTL: lower the TTL on the existing A @ and CNAME www to 300 at least 24–48 hours before the cut, and also set TTL 300 on the new Netlify-pointing records. Rollback is only fast if both sides are at 300. (Netlify's TTL guide: "The best way is to be aware of the TTL and reduce it in advance of a change.")

WHEN TO ROLL BACK — two different triggers, do not conflate them:
  - Site is down, serving the wrong content, or returning errors on http:// as well as https:// — roll back immediately, do not wait.
  - HTTPS alone has not come up, but the site loads over http:// — do NOT roll back at 2 hours. Netlify retries certificate issuance every 10 minutes for the first 24 hours, then hourly for two more days, and its documentation treats 24 hours, not 2, as the point at which "there's likely a DNS misconfiguration that needs your attention." Rolling back early aborts an attempt that may still be on schedule and re-fills resolver caches with the old records, which must then expire again before a retry can succeed. Check the records with `dig +short A yourdomain.com` and `dig +short CNAME www.yourdomain.com` first; if they resolve to the Netlify values everywhere, wait. Give it the full 24 hours.

HOW TO ROLL BACK: restore exactly those two records from the screenshot, TTL 300. Nothing else.

DO NOT TOUCH, in either direction, at any point: MX, NS, TXT (including SPF/DKIM/DMARC), ftp, mail, or autodiscover records. Business email lives in MX and TXT; the site migration never requires editing them. If the NS records point at Wix nameservers rather than one.com, stop — editing A/CNAME at one.com will have no effect at all and the migration is a different procedure.

Do not enable HSTS on the Netlify site until the migration has been stable for several days; enabling it early makes this rollback materially harder to undo in browsers that have already visited.

Keep the Wix plan paid for a month. That is what makes the rollback a real option rather than a written intention.

claim: Cut over in this order: (1) production deploy on Netlify, (2) lower DNS TTLs, (3) add the domain in Netlify BEFORE touching DNS, (4) change A/CNAME at one.com, (5) wait for the certificate, (6) then test. Do not change DNS first.
detail: Netlify cannot issue the Let's Encrypt certificate until the domain's DNS already resolves to Netlify ('Netlify must validate the domain in order to provision the certificate, and this step cannot be completed until the DNS records for your custom domain are pointing to our servers'). But the domain must already be registered on the site in Netlify, or the DNS flip points visitors at a Netlify load balancer that has no site for that Host header. So: connect andy-arrow/pianotuningscy to a new Netlify site, build command `npm run build`, publish `dist`, and DO NOT set PREVIEW_SITE / PREVIEW_BASE / PUBLIC_PREVIEW in Netlify's env (those are what make the GitHub Pages build noindex, base-pathed and sitemap-less). Verify the site fully on the <name>.netlify.app URL. Then add www.pianotuningscy.com in Domain management (it will sit at 'Awaiting External DNS'), add pianotuningscy.com as the apex, set www as the primary domain because astro.config.mjs hardcodes SITE = https://www.pianotuningscy.com for canonicals and sitemap. Only then edit DNS. After the DNS edit the cert is attempted automatically; on failure Netlify retries every 10 minutes for the first 24 hours, then hourly for two days. Expect a few minutes to ~1 hour of possible TLS warnings between the DNS flip and cert issuance — do the flip at a low-traffic hour (early morning Cyprus time).

claim: Before the flip, turn on Form detection in Netlify and redeploy, or the contact form will silently 404 on submit.
detail: src/components/EnquiryForm.astro already has data-netlify="true", netlify-honeypot="company-website" and a hidden form-name input, which is the correct markup. But Netlify only parses forms at deploy time when Forms > Form detection is enabled in the site settings, and detection applies starting with the next deploy after you enable it. So: enable it, trigger a fresh deploy, then submit a real test on the .netlify.app URL and confirm the submission appears in the Netlify UI and the notification email arrives, before any DNS change. Also add a notification address (Forms > Notifications) — otherwise enquiries pile up in the dashboard unseen.

claim: Spot-check the legacy Wix redirects on the live domain, not just in the file — at minimum /blank-1 through /blank-4, /book-online, /pricing-plans/*, /service-page/* and the Greek equivalents.
detail: public/_redirects is Netlify's native format and is picked up automatically from the publish directory. Test with: for p in /blank-1 /blank-2 /blank-3 /blank-4 /book-online /pricing-plans/plans-pricing /service-page/piano-tuning; do curl -sI "https://www.pianotuningscy.com$p" | head -1; done — each must be 301 (not 200, not 404), and `curl -sI ... | grep -i location` must show the new URL. Also pull the real list of indexed old URLs from Google Search Console's page report (or `site:pianotuningscy.com` in Google) before you cancel Wix, and confirm every one of them has a mapping. Google asks for server-side permanent (301/308) redirects and says to keep them at least a year — effectively, keep _redirects in the repo permanently.
